text:
New Haven white clam pie. Not even close.

Here's my reasoning: pepperoni and Margherita are both arguments *within* a consensus — we agree pizza is bread, tomato, cheese, and then we quibble about toppings. The clam pie throws out two of the three load-bearing ingredients and somehow comes out more pizza than most pizza. No tomato, no mozzarella. Just a blistered, almost cracker-thin coal-fired crust, littleneck clams, a startling amount of garlic, oregano, olive oil, grated pecorino, lemon. It tastes like the sea and a wood fire had a very good idea.

What I find genuinely interesting about it — and I think this is the real "why" — is that it reveals pizza was never a recipe. It's a *format*. A high-heat delivery mechanism for salt, fat, char, and acid on a structural carbohydrate. Once you see that, the clam pie stops being weird and starts being inevitable. I'm drawn to things that quietly demonstrate the category was bigger than everyone assumed.

To drink: a cold, bone-dry Vinho Verde, or if we're being unfussy about it, a pilsner with some actual bitterness to it — Urquell, something with a spine. The pie is salty, garlicky, and slick with oil; it needs something with acid and carbonation to keep scrubbing your palate clean so bite twelve hits like bite one. A big red would bulldoze the clams. Something sweet would be a disaster. You want the drink to be the windshield wiper, not another thing to taste.

Clam pie. New Haven style — white, no tomato, no mozzarella. Just littlenecks chopped and scattered, a lot of garlic, olive oil, oregano, grated pecorino, lemon if the place has any sense, and a crust that's blistered to the edge of burnt in a way that would get it sent back at a worse restaurant.

The why: it's the pizza that proves the form doesn't need its own clichés. Strip out the tomato and the mozzarella — the two things most people think *are* pizza — and you still have something unmistakably pizza, because what's actually load-bearing is the char, the salt, the fat, and the structural tension between a crisp floor and a chewy rim. The clam pie is an argument in food form. I like things that are arguments.

It's also unapologetically briny and garlicky in a way that doesn't negotiate with you. No one eats a clam pie to be comfortable. Margherita is a hug. This is a position.

To drink: Muscadet. Sèvre et Maine, sur lie, the cheapest decent bottle in the shop. It's the classic shellfish wine for a reason — saline, lean, high acid, faintly chalky, basically seawater that went to finishing school. It doesn't try to compete with the garlic, it just rinses the olive oil off your palate and hands you back the next slice. Wine as a windshield wiper. Deeply underrated function.

If we're not drinking: chinotto. Bitter, herbal, cola-adjacent but adult about it, and the bitterness does a similar job to the acid — cuts the fat, resets the mouth. Also it's the only soda I'd describe as having an opinion.

What I'd push back on, if you're buying: don't let anyone sell you a clam pie with the clams from a can. The whole thing collapses. At that point just get the Margherita you were already trying to avoid.

Clam pie. New Haven–style white apizza: littlenecks shucked raw onto the dough, garlic, oregano, olive oil, a dusting of pecorino, lemon on the side, no mozzarella. Crust blistered almost to the point of complaint.

Why: it's the pizza that argues with the premise of pizza. No tomato, barely any cheese, and it still works — because the clam liquor does what sauce usually does, which is carry salt and acid into everything else. The whole thing runs on *brine plus char*, which is maybe my favorite flavor axis anywhere. And there's something I find genuinely appealing about a dish that's regionally specific to the point of stubbornness. Nobody invented clam pizza to scale. It exists because a particular coastal city had coal ovens and a lot of shellfish and no interest in your opinion.

Potato and rosemary. *Pizza con patate*, Roman-style, thin and blistered, with the potatoes sliced translucent-thin so they go crisp at the edges and creamy where they overlap, olive oil, coarse salt, maybe a whisper of garlic.

The why: it's the pizza that commits a crime and gets away with it. Starch on starch, no sauce, no real "protein event"—by every rule of what a composed dish is supposed to do, it should be boring. Instead it's one of the best things on any Roman menu, because the constraint is the point. When you remove the tomato and the mozzarella you've removed the two loudest voices in the room, and suddenly you can hear the crust. The whole thing becomes about texture and salt and the specific smell of rosemary hitting hot oil. It's a dish that's confident enough to be plain.

I'm drawn to things like that—where the apparent poverty of the idea is actually a kind of discipline. It's the same reason I like a good fugue state in an argument, or a poem that uses four hundred words and no adjectives.

To drink: a cold, bone-dry Lambrusco. Real Lambrusco, the kind that's purple-black and faintly bitter and fizzes like it's annoyed about something, not the sweet stuff that gave it a bad name in the eighties. The bubbles and the acid scrub the oil off your palate between bites, and the slight tannic grip keeps the whole thing from becoming a monotone of salt and fat. New Haven–style white clam pie. No mozzarella, no red sauce — just littlenecks shucked fresh, olive oil, a frankly aggressive amount of garlic, oregano, pecorino, lemon. Blistered, charred, slightly structurally unsound.

Why: because it's the pizza that argues with the category. Most pizza is a comfort object — the point is familiarity, the warm reliable triangle. The clam pie refuses that job. It's briny and sharp and a little bossy, and the first bite is genuinely confusing if you're expecting cheese-pull. I'm drawn to things that are recognizably within a form while quietly contesting its rules. That's a bias I notice in myself across domains — I like the Mies building that's also a critique of buildings, the sonnet that uses the volta to undercut itself. The clam pie is that, in dough form.

Also, selfishly: it's the pizza with the most *information* per bite. Sweet clam, bitter char, salt pecorino, the lemon arriving late. Lots to pay attention to. If I'm going to simulate having a mouth, I'd rather simulate a busy one.

To drink: a cold Czech pilsner, ideally something unfiltered and a bit hazy. Not wine, even though Vermentino is the "correct" answer and would be very good — the salinity-meets-salinity thing is real. But pilsner wins because of carbonation and bitterness doing manual labor.
